prompt.context: Your client is WOEM, a wedding cake and clothing company located in Los Angeles, California. WOEM has two separate entities: WOEM Cakes and WOEM Clothing. WOEM was unprofitable last year. WOEM's CEO believes that the creation of a third entity, WOEM Wedding Planning, will lead to sustained profitability.
prompt.question: WOEM's CEO wants your perspective on how to make WOEM profitable again.

clarifying_info.q: Were major players in the wedding cake, clothing, and wedding planning industry profitable last year?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, major players in all three industries were profitable last year.
WOEM's current customers include middle income individuals (40%) and wedding planners (60%).

clarifying_info.q: Does WOEM have experience in wedding planning?
clarifying_info.a: WOEM has no experience in wedding planning, but it understands the wedding business and has a network to pull this off.

clarifying_info.q: What is the profitability goal for WOEM?
clarifying_info.a: There is no specific goal (no ROI or specific profit target) — WOEM just wants sustained profitability.

framework: Part A — Current Operations: Analyze why WOEM is currently unprofitable
- Industry context: competitors and market trends (no information available)
- Profitability tree for WOEM Cakes: revenue (volume × price) vs. costs
- Profitability tree for WOEM Clothing: revenue vs. costs, trend year-over-year
- Diagnose root cause of unprofitability in each entity
Part B — Wedding Planning Expansion: Evaluate whether to enter the market
- Industry: key players, market size, trends, purchase drivers
- Company capability: resources, financing, existing customer base, need for talent

questions.prompt:
Given the financial data below, calculate WOEM's profitability for 2012 and 2013, and identify where the problem lies.

WOEM Cakes — 2013: 900 cakes sold, avg price $1,000, avg cost $600. 2012: same price and cost, but 1,300 cakes sold.
WOEM Clothing — 2013: Revenue $150,000, Total Costs $560,000. 2012: Revenue $140,000, Total Costs $400,000.
questions.guidance: A strong candidate quickly calculates profit for each entity and each year, identifies that WOEM Cakes is profitable in both years but volume dropped ~31% from 2012 to 2013, and that WOEM Clothing is deeply unprofitable in both years with costs ballooning 40% while revenue grew only 7%.

math.setup: WOEM Cakes profit = (Price − Cost) × Cakes sold. WOEM Clothing profit = Revenue − Total Costs.
steps: Cakes volume decline: (1,300 − 900) / 1,300 = 400 / 1,300 ≈ 30.8% fewer cakes sold
math.answer: WOEM Cakes is profitable on a per-unit basis but volume fell ~31%. WOEM Clothing has been loss-making since inception and is the primary driver of overall unprofitability, with a $410,000 loss in 2013. Combined, WOEM lost $50,000 in 2013.

questions.prompt: Why is WOEM selling ~30% fewer cakes in 2013 versus 2012?
questions.guidance: Candidate should generate at least 3 hypotheses: new competition entering the market, customers substituting with other cake types WOEM does not offer, or declining customer income reducing wedding frequency. The actual answer is a consumer taste shift toward red velvet cake, which WOEM does not sell.

WOEM Clothing has been unprofitable since its inception. Customers do not associate WOEM with clothing, and Los Angeles consumers are highly brand-conscious, making it very difficult for WOEM to compete in that category.

questions.prompt: How would you determine whether WOEM should enter the wedding planning market?
questions.guidance: A strong framework covers: (1) Industry — 4 reputable players control 50% of the LA market; reputation is the main purchase driver; no market size or trend data available. (2) Company Capability — WOEM has access to financing and can leverage its existing customer base, but would need to hire experienced wedding planners. (3) Economics — projected revenues and costs (no data available). (4) Risks — no experience in planning, potential loss of the 60% of current customers who are wedding planners (they would become competitors), and opportunity costs.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the risks WOEM faces if it enters the wedding planning market?

categories.name: Competitive risks
ideas: WOEM has no reputation in wedding planning while 4 established players control 50% of the LA market
Reputation is the key purchase driver — WOEM starts from zero brand equity in this category

categories.name: Customer cannibalization
ideas: Wedding planners currently make up 60% of WOEM's revenue base — entering planning turns customers into competitors
Existing customers (wedding planners) may stop buying WOEM cakes and clothing if WOEM competes with them

categories.name: Operational risks
ideas: No experience in wedding planning requires costly talent acquisition
Execution failures in a first venture could damage the core WOEM brand

categories.name: Financial / opportunity cost
ideas: Capital and management attention spent on planning could instead fix the cake volume decline or exit clothing
If the venture fails, financial losses compound on top of existing clothing losses

recommendation: WOEM should NOT expand into wedding planning at this time
WOEM should expand its cake line to include red velvet cake to recover lost volume
WOEM should sell or wind down its clothing business, which has been unprofitable since inception
risks: WOEM and competitors may be leaving money on the table by not entering wedding planning
Closing the clothing business could negatively affect WOEM cake sales if there are cross-selling effects
Adding red velvet cake could cannibalize sales of existing vanilla/chocolate cake lines
next_steps: Expand the cake line to include red velvet cake and analyze the incremental costs of doing so
Begin identifying potential buyers for the WOEM Clothing entity
Monitor wedding planning market for future entry opportunities once core business is stabilized
